description: Rivets, threaded fastenings, soft soldering, brazing and welding — temperatures, fillers and when to use each.
content_html:
Permanent and Temporary Joining

Engineering assemblies require parts to be joined. The choice of method depends on whether the joint needs to be dismantled later, the materials being joined, the load the joint must carry and the cost of the process. Joining methods divide into two families: permanent (riveting, soldering, brazing, welding — joint cannot be undone without damaging the parts) and temporary (threaded fastenings such as bolts and screws — joint can be taken apart and reassembled). Understanding this distinction, and the temperature and filler requirements of each thermal process, is the key to answering exam questions correctly.

Riveting

Rivets are used to permanently join two or more sheets of metal. Pop (blind) rivets are used where only one side of the joint is accessible — common in aircraft skins and bodywork. Solid rivets require access to both sides: a bucking bar supports the tail while a rivet gun deforms it into a second head.

The correct sequence for riveting is one of the most-tested topics in the examination. Many students omit the marking-out stage and go straight to drilling, which means they lose marks. The full sequence is:

  1. Mark out — use a scriber and rule to mark the rivet positions on the top sheet.
  2. Centre-punch each marked position to prevent the drill wandering.
  3. Clamp the sheets together in the correct position.
  4. Drill the rivet holes through both sheets using a twist drill of the correct diameter.
  5. De-burr the holes to remove sharp edges.
  6. Insert the rivet through the aligned holes.
  7. Form the tail — use a rivet snap (or for pop rivets, the rivet gun) to peen (deform) the tail into the second head, clamping the sheets together.
Key Fact

The riveting sequence always starts with marking out. Skipping this stage — going directly from “select rivet” to “drill” — is the single most common error on joining questions and costs marks every year.

Threaded Fastenings (Temporary Joining)

Bolts, machine screws and set screws are threaded fastenings. A bolt passes through clearance holes in both parts and is secured by a nut on the reverse; a machine screw threads into a tapped hole in one part. Threaded fastenings are temporary: they can be removed with a spanner or screwdriver, which makes them essential for assemblies that need maintenance access — such as engine covers, gearbox housings and electrical panels. Locking devices (spring washers, nyloc nuts, thread-locking adhesive) prevent vibration-induced loosening.

Soft Soldering

Soft soldering uses a filler metal with a melting point below 450 °C — traditionally a tin-lead alloy, now typically lead-free tin-copper or tin-silver for health reasons. The soldering iron heats the joint; flux is applied to remove oxide films and allow the solder to flow; the filler melts and fills the gap by capillary action. The parent metal does not melt. Soft solder is used for electronic circuit-board connections and for joining copper water pipes (plumbing). The joint is weaker than the parent metal and not suitable for structural applications.

Hard soldering (also called silver soldering) uses a filler alloy containing silver, with a melting point between 450 °C and 900 °C. The process is otherwise similar to soft soldering — the parent metal is not melted — but the joint is significantly stronger and more heat-resistant. Hard soldering is used to join copper and brass components in plumbing and jewellery.

Brazing uses a brass filler rod (typically 60% copper, 40% zinc) with a melting point around 870 °C to join steel or copper parts. A blowtorch or oxy-acetylene torch heats the joint area to the correct temperature (cherry-red for steel). Flux is applied to prevent oxidation. The filler rod is touched to the hot joint and melts into the gap by capillary action — the engineer must NOT melt the filler directly in the flame. The parent metal is not melted. This is the critical distinction: brazing uses a filler rod at a temperature below the parent metal’s melting point. Welding (below) melts the parent metal itself.

A common exam error is confusing soft soldering and brazing. The temperature is the key: soft solder < 450 °C; brazing > 450 °C (typically 870 °C for brass filler). Another error is confusing brazing with welding: in brazing, the parent metal remains solid; in welding, the parent metal melts.

Welding

Welding is the only joining process listed here in which the parent metal melts. An electric arc or oxy-acetylene flame generates temperatures above the melting point of the steel (above 1,500 °C), creating a molten pool at the joint. A filler rod (or the wire electrode in MIG welding) adds material to the pool, which solidifies into a continuous fusion bond on cooling.

Common welding processes:

  • MIG (Metal Inert Gas) welding — a continuously fed wire electrode melts into the joint, shielded by an inert gas (argon or CO₂) to exclude oxygen. MIG is fast, highly controllable and widely used in vehicle body repair and fabrication workshops. BAE Systems uses MIG welding for structural steel fabrication on ships and aircraft ground equipment.
  • Arc (manual metal arc) welding — a coated electrode is clamped into a holder; the arc between electrode and workpiece melts both the electrode coating (which provides a flux) and the parent metal. Slower than MIG but requires no gas supply, making it portable for site work.
Key Fact

Soft soldering < 450 °C, parent metal not melted. Brazing > 450 °C (brass filler rod), parent metal not melted. Welding: parent metal melts — this is what distinguishes it from all other thermal joining methods.

Soft soldering: temp < 450 °C | filler: tin alloy | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: copper, steel, PCB | use: electronics, plumbing

Hard soldering / silver soldering: temp 450–900 °C | filler: silver alloy | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: copper, brass | use: plumbing, jewellery

Brazing: temp ~870 °C | filler: brass rod | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: steel, copper | use: pipework, bicycle frames, small engineering assemblies

Welding (MIG/arc): temp > 1500 °C | filler: electrode wire | parent metal: MELTS | materials: steel (MIG/arc), aluminium (MIG) | use: structures, vehicles, fabrication
exam_tip_html: For any joining question, first decide: permanent or temporary? Then for thermal joining, sort by temperature and whether the parent metal melts. Soft soldering: <450 °C, parent metal intact. Brazing: ~870 °C, brass filler, parent metal intact. Welding: parent metal melts. If you write “brazing melts the parent metal” or “welding uses a filler rod at low temperature” you have mixed up these two processes and will lose marks. For riveting questions, always include marking out as the first step — examiners penalise its absence every year.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Riveting is a permanent mechanical joint; the sequence is mark out → centre punch → clamp → drill → de-burr → insert rivet → form tail. Never skip marking out.
  • Threaded fastenings (bolts, screws) are temporary. Soft soldering (<450 °C) and brazing (~870 °C, brass filler rod) both leave the parent metal solid. Only welding melts the parent metal.
  • MIG welding uses a continuously fed wire electrode shielded by inert gas; arc welding uses a coated electrode and requires no gas. Both melt the parent metal and produce a strong permanent fusion bond.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the brazing process?
A) A filler rod is melted by direct flame contact to form the joint
B) A brass filler rod melts into the joint at around 870 °C while the parent metal remains solid
C) The parent metal is melted and fused together without a filler material
D) A low-melting-point tin alloy is applied below 450 °C to join PCB components
practice_questions.marks: B) A brass filler rod melts into the joint at around 870 °C while the parent metal remains solid [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between brazing and welding.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any two of:
- Brazing uses a filler rod (brass); welding melts the parent metal itself (may or may not add filler wire)
- Brazing temperature (~870 °C) is below the parent metal melting point; welding exceeds the parent metal melting point (>1500 °C for steel)
- Brazing leaves the parent metal solid; welding fuses the parent metal into a molten pool
- Brazing is typically used for thinner or dissimilar sections; welding produces a higher-strength structural bond
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages involved in riveting two steel plates together. Your answer must include all stages in the correct order.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four stages in correct order. Marking out must be included:
1. Mark out rivet positions using a scriber and rule [must be present]
2. Centre-punch each marked position
3. Clamp the plates together in position
4. Drill rivet holes through both plates with a twist drill
5. De-burr the holes to remove sharp edges
6. Insert rivets through the aligned holes
7. Form/peen the tail into a second head using a rivet snap or rivet gun
[4 marks — deduct a mark if marking out is absent, as stated in examiner guidance]

practice_questions.text:
Complete the sentences below using the correct words from the list.

Brazing / Welding / Soft soldering / Threaded fastening / Riveting

(a) _____ is the only thermal joining process in which the parent metal melts.
(b) _____ uses a brass filler rod at approximately 870 °C without melting the parent metal.
(c) A bolt and nut is an example of a _____, which allows the joint to be disassembled.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Welding [1 mark]
(b) Brazing [1 mark]
(c) Threaded fastening [1 mark]
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Thornfield Fabrications Ltd is producing a mild steel frame for an industrial machine guard. The joints must be strong and permanent. The production supervisor is deciding between MIG welding and brazing.

Evaluate which joining method is more suitable for this application. In your answer consider: joint strength, material compatibility, temperature, production speed and operator skill required.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clear evaluation of both methods against the specific scenario (mild steel frame, strong permanent joint, industrial machine guard). Advantages and limitations of each addressed. Justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both methods covered with some comparison. Most factors addressed. Conclusion present.

Developing (3-4 marks): One method described in detail; comparison limited. Scenario details used minimally.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic points with little reference to the scenario.

Content that may be credited:
MIG welding: melts the mild steel parent metal to form a full-penetration fusion bond — very strong, suitable for a structural machine guard frame. Fast deposition rate; suitable for thick steel sections; requires shielding gas supply and operator trained to AWS/CSWIP standard. HAZ (heat-affected zone) may distort thin sections.
Brazing: brass filler at ~870 °C, parent metal does not melt — joint is weaker than a MIG weld for structural steel; not ideal for a heavy machine guard frame under dynamic load. Advantages: less distortion, no shielding gas, smaller heat input.
Conclusion: MIG welding is the better choice for a structural mild steel machine guard frame requiring a strong, permanent joint. Brazing would be suitable for lighter, non-structural assemblies such as pipe fittings or bicycle frames.

practice_questions.text: Give two advantages of using threaded fastenings (bolts and nuts) rather than welding to join the access panels on an industrial machine.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any two of:
- Panels can be removed for maintenance or inspection without damaging the frame
- No specialist equipment (welder, shielding gas) is needed for assembly or disassembly
- Damaged panels can be individually replaced rather than cutting welds
- Assembly can take place on-site without a welder
[2 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the first stage of the riveting sequence that students most often omit?
At what approximate temperature does brazing occur, and does it melt the parent metal?
options: Below 450 °C; the parent metal does not melt
Around 870 °C; the parent metal does not melt

knowledge_checks.q: Welding is distinguished from brazing because in welding the _____ melts at the joint.
MIG welding shields the molten pool from oxygen using a flow of _____ gas such as argon or CO2.
Match each joining method to its key characteristic:
right: Tin alloy filler below 450 °C; parent metal not melted; used for PCBs and plumbing
Brass filler rod ~870 °C; parent metal not melted; used for steel and copper
Parent metal melts; produces a strong fusion bond for structural steel

flashcard_questions.q: What is the first stage of riveting that is most often omitted by students?
flashcard_questions.a: Marking out the rivet positions with a scriber and rule.
A permanent fastener with a pre-formed head; the tail is deformed (peened) to clamp sheets together.

flashcard_questions.q: How do threaded fastenings differ from rivets in terms of joint type?
flashcard_questions.a: Threaded fastenings are temporary (can be undone); rivets make a permanent joint.

flashcard_questions.q: At what temperature does soft solder melt?
What filler material is used in brazing?
Does brazing melt the parent metal?
flashcard_questions.a: No — only the brass filler rod melts; the parent metal stays solid.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes welding unique among thermal joining methods?
flashcard_questions.a: It is the only method that melts the parent metal at the joint.

flashcard_questions.q: What does MIG stand for in MIG welding?
What is the purpose of flux in soldering and brazing?
flashcard_questions.a: It removes oxide films from the metal surface so the filler can bond cleanly.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are locking devices used with threaded fastenings in machinery?
flashcard_questions.a: To prevent vibration from gradually loosening the bolt or nut during operation.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one application where soft soldering is used.
flashcard_questions.a: Joining components on a printed circuit board (PCB) or joining copper water pipes.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is brazing suitable for joining bicycle frame tubes?
flashcard_questions.a: It produces a strong joint without melting the thin steel tubes, reducing the risk of distortion.

glossary_terms.definition: A permanent mechanical fastener consisting of a cylindrical shank with a pre-formed head on one end; the tail end is deformed (peened) to clamp two or more sheets together.
Fasteners with a helical thread that allow two or more parts to be clamped together and later separated without damaging the parts.
A joining process that uses a low-melting-point filler alloy (below 450 °C) to join metals, typically tin-copper or tin-silver alloy; the parent metal is not melted.
A joining process that uses a brass filler rod to join steel or copper components at temperatures above 450 °C; the parent metal is not melted.
A permanent joining process in which the parent metals at the joint are melted together, usually with the addition of a filler metal, to form a fusion bond.
